title: Registry Data in Epidemiology: Opportunities and Challenges

yaml.title: Registry Data in Epidemiology: Opportunities and Challenges
yaml.description: Administrative and population registries are transforming large-scale health research — but they come with real limitations that researchers need to reckon with.

markdown.markdown:
Population registries — particularly those maintained by national statistical agencies and health authorities in countries like the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, and Finland — represent a remarkable resource for epidemiological research. When a child is born, that birth is registered. When someone moves, the change of address is recorded. When a patient is admitted to hospital, the diagnosis codes follow them. When a prescription is dispensed, it is logged.

Linked across domains, these data yield a longitudinal picture of an entire population's life course: where people live, how they move, what they earn, how healthy they are, what treatments they receive, and what happens to them over decades. The scale is unlike anything achievable through prospective study design — not a sample of thousands, but entire national populations of millions.

I have worked extensively with linked registry data from Statistics Netherlands (CBS), which integrates population registration, income and wealth records, educational attainment, employment history, and healthcare utilization across time. For my PhD research, this meant linking residential addresses to spatially resolved air pollution estimates for over 12 million adults — an analysis that would simply not be possible with conventional cohort data.

## The Genuine Strengths

**Scale and completeness.** Coverage of entire populations eliminates selection bias at enrollment. Everyone is included — not just those healthy enough or motivated enough to participate in a traditional cohort.

**Longitudinal depth.** Registry data typically spans decades. This makes it possible to study long latency periods, cumulative exposures, and outcomes that take years to manifest.

**Rare outcomes.** With millions of individuals under observation, even genuinely rare outcomes occur often enough to estimate effects with precision. This is critical for studying diseases like specific cancer subtypes, or rare cardiovascular events.

**Multiple domains.** Linkage across registries means you can characterize the same individual across health, socioeconomic, residential, and occupational dimensions simultaneously — approximating the exposome rather than studying single exposures in isolation.

**No attrition.** Prospective cohorts lose participants over time, and attrition is rarely random. Registry data does not suffer from this in the same way; administrative records follow individuals regardless of their engagement.

## The Real Limitations

None of this comes without cost.

**Data collected for administrative, not scientific, purposes.** This is the original sin of registry research. Diagnosis codes are assigned for billing or administrative purposes, not for research validity. ICD codes are imprecise, can reflect coding habits as much as clinical reality, and change with coding system updates. Exposure variables that matter scientifically — lifestyle factors, diet, physical activity, detailed clinical measurements — are typically absent entirely.

**Unmeasured confounding.** Because of the above, registry studies often cannot adequately control for important confounders. A study of drug effectiveness using claims data may not be able to adjust for disease severity, functional status, or the reasons a clinician chose one treatment over another (channeling bias and confounding by indication are endemic in pharmacoepidemiology).

**Measurement error in exposures.** When spatial models are used to assign air pollution exposures based on residential address, that is at best a proxy for actual personal exposure. People spend time away from home; indoor environments differ from outdoor measurements; the resolution of the model has limits.

**Ecological fallacy.** When individual-level data is unavailable and neighborhood-level data is used instead, associations at the area level may not reflect relationships at the individual level. This matters particularly when studying socioeconomic effects.

**Privacy and access constraints.** In many countries, access to linked administrative data is tightly controlled. In the Netherlands, all analyses on CBS microdata must be conducted within a secure remote access environment; no data leaves the system. This protects privacy but creates practical constraints on workflow, reproducibility, and international collaboration.

## How to Work Responsibly with Registry Data

A few principles I've found useful:

**Be explicit about what your variables actually measure.** A "welfare benefit receipt" variable is not the same as socioeconomic position — it's a proxy with specific coverage patterns, eligibility rules, and time lags. The same applies to diagnosis codes, which capture recorded diagnoses, not underlying disease.

**Use multiple indicators wherever possible.** No single administrative variable captures a construct fully. Using education, income, wealth, and employment status as separate and complementary indicators of socioeconomic position produces a richer and more robust characterization than any single measure.

**Invest in validation.** Where linkage to external data with gold-standard measurement is possible — even for a subsample — it's worth doing. Validation studies that quantify the sensitivity and specificity of registry-derived variables inform what can and cannot be concluded.

**Report what you can't measure.** Transparency about unmeasured confounders, missing variables, and the limitations of proxy measures is not just good practice — it's what makes findings credible.

## The Dutch Infrastructure as a Model

The Netherlands offers an unusually well-developed registry infrastructure for health research. The possibility of linking Statistics Netherlands microdata with air pollution dispersion models, hospital discharge records, and municipal demographic data in a single privacy-preserving environment is the kind of resource that makes studies like mine possible. Similar infrastructure exists in Scandinavia, with active efforts to build comparable systems in other European countries.

For researchers interested in leveraging these resources, the practical investment is real: navigating access procedures, data governance requirements, and the technical environments takes time. But the scientific return — the ability to study an entire population across years and domains — is hard to match any other way.
